title: How Cinnamon Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore cinnamon: its history from ancient texts and funeral pyres to Roman prices, the Portuguese and Dutch role in the Sri Lankan cinnamon trade, the main types (true cinnamon/Ceylon, cassia, and others), how cinnamon is harvested from inner bark, grading and storage, culinary uses, health claims including antioxidants, antimicrobial properties, blood sugar and diabetes, and the coumarin toxicity risk and the cinnamon challenge. The episode opens with banter (small-batch rye, cigars, a pet flea preventative) and closes with listener mail thank-yous.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener mail

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about small-batch rye sourced from a single Indiana factory, cigar smoking, a pet flea preventative, and football, then introduce cinnamon as the topic.

segments.title: Cinnamon history and ancient uses
segments.summary: Cinnamon is tree bark, and it appears in writing as early as the 1st century BC in a Chinese botanical text. Uses mentioned include Moses' anointing oil, Egyptian embalming, and funeral pyres. Pliny says a pound cost about ten months' wages for an average Roman, and Nero burned a year's supply at his wife's funeral.

segments.title: Spice trade prices and cassia substitution
segments.summary: Cinnamon prices fell by the late eighteenth century as cassia from Indonesia, Vietnam and China was sold in Europe as a substitute for true cinnamon. A Roman emperor had set maximum prices. The hosts compare spice costs then and now.

segments.title: Types of cinnamon
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish true cinnamon (Ceylon, from Sri Lanka) from cassia. Cassia is cheaper and stronger, and is what is common in the US and Canada, while Ceylon is more common in Mexico and Europe. Ceylon is subtler and works well in teas, and cassia can fade into the background of dishes. Over a hundred wild cinnamon species are mentioned.

segments.title: Harvesting and history of the Sri Lankan trade
segments.summary: Cinnamon is harvested from the inner bark of cut-back shoots, which are dried and curled into quills. Historically, a low caste in Sri Lanka harvested it. The Portuguese found the source and enslaved workers, and the Dutch later continued that control, and then cultivation was tried elsewhere. Quill grading uses diameter categories: Alba, Continental, and Zahambug.

segments.title: Cooking with cinnamon and storage
segments.summary: Hosts discuss grinding quills versus cassia, their own cooking with cinnamon, and its use historically for savory meat dishes in medieval Europe before it moved to desserts. They cover curries and chili, and storage: whole sticks keep about a year, ground cinnamon about half that.

segments.title: Health benefits, risks and the cinnamon challenge
segments.summary: Hosts cover antioxidants and free radicals, cinnamon's antimicrobial and antiseptic properties from cinnamaldehyde, and the Middle Ages thieves oil. They warn that coumarin can harm the liver and kidneys, that cinnamon dust can cause asthma, and that possible blood sugar benefits for type 2 diabetes need care with cassia. They warn against the cinnamon challenge, which led to 178 poison control calls in the first six months of 2012.

segments.title: Listener mail thank-yous
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners for gifts including Hawaiian sea salt, books, a whoopee cushion, coffee, mugs, candy, and illustrations, and they give contact details.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing remarks and how to contact the show on Twitter, Facebook, email, and the website.
